title: Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308)
hookLine: every creature has its own thisness, loved by God

cards: Two sparrows land on a fence. Same kind, same size, same brown feathers, same tilt of the head. A bird book would describe them in exactly the same words.
And yet one is this sparrow, and the other is that one. If one flies away, the one left behind isn't a copy. It's itself.

What makes it that? That small question, the kind a child might ask, occupied the teachers of the Middle Ages, and one Franciscan friar gave it an answer that came to be known by a strange, lovely word.

teach.b: The friar is John Duns Scotus, a teacher at Oxford and Paris, remembered as the Subtle Doctor. For him and for Thomas Aquinas alike, the two sparrows share one nature: they're both sparrows.
The question was what makes each one an individual. Aquinas, the Dominican teacher, pointed to matter: this sparrow is made of this bit of the world, and that one of that bit.
Scotus thought there had to be something more. Something positive in each creature that belongs to it alone, not a leftover, not a label, but the real heart of its being this one.
The Latin word tied to his teaching is haecceitas.
In English, haecceity: thisness. Why would a friar care? Because of Francis, who didn't love birds in general.
He talked to these birds, on this road, and called one particular wolf his brother. Scotus gives that habit a philosophy.
If each creature has its own thisness, then God doesn't make and love things in bulk, as samples of a kind.

teach.h: GOD LOVES EACH ONE AS ITSELF.
teach.b: God knows and wills each one as itself. Jesus says something close in the gospel: not one sparrow is forgotten before God, and even the hairs of your head are numbered.

teach.h: CALLED THEE BY THY NAME: THOU ART MINE.
teach.b: And the prophet Isaiah hears God say, in the Douay-Rheims, "called thee by thy name: thou art mine."
Much later the poet Gerard Manley Hopkins, a Jesuit priest, took Scotus to heart and wrote poems about each thing crying out its own self. Readers still weigh Scotus's answer against Aquinas's.
But on Scotus's account, nobody is a duplicate. Not the sparrow, not you.

how: Franciscans study Duns Scotus as one of their order's great teachers, and the Church has beatified him as Blessed John Duns Scotus.

o: the shared nature that makes a sparrow a sparrow
thisness: what makes each thing itself and no other
a holy habit built up slowly through daily practice

games.q: Scotus and thisness — tap the pairs.

s: for Scotus, two creatures of the same kind are interchangeable
each has its own thisness, something positive that is its alone.
Aquinas and Scotus answered the question differently
Aquinas pointed to matter; Scotus to each thing's own thisness. Catholics honor both.
haecceity means a creature's kind or species
it means the opposite: not what kind it is, but this one.

games.q: you're a medieval teacher. two sparrows share the same nature, size and color. what makes this one this one?
o: the bit of matter each is made of.
something in each that is its very own: its thisness.
games.why: that's Scotus's answer, haecceity. Aquinas pointed to matter instead, and the Church honors both teachers.

practice: Pick one thing near you, a mug, a leaf, your own hand, and instead of the category it belongs to, look at this one: the chip on the rim, the particular vein, the scar on the knuckle.

Keep looking until it stops being a mug and becomes this mug, the only one with exactly this history. If you pray, thank God for making it, and you, one at a time; if you don't, simply let it be itself.

wordCard.voice: Haecceity. Duns Scotus's thisness: what makes each creature itself and no other, known and loved by God. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: thisness, the word tied to Scotus's teaching on what makes each thing itself.

carryVoice: Your line: this one. On Scotus's account, God makes nothing in bulk. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: called thee by thy name: thou art mine.
